name: LL-37
lead: LL-37 is a 37-amino-acid antimicrobial peptide and the only cathelicidin made by humans. It is cleaved from a precursor protein, hCAP18, and is produced by neutrophils and epithelial cells including skin keratinocytes [3][4]. It is part of the innate immune system and also signals to immune cells [3].

In appearance communities it is sometimes discussed as a research peptide for acne or skin quality. Published work is predominantly on its natural role in skin infection and inflammatory skin disease, including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea, rather than on LL-37 as a cosmetic treatment [1][5]. No clinical trial of LL-37 for acne or cosmetic skin improvement was found.

paras: LL-37 is released from hCAP18 by proteolytic cleavage and acts on microbial membranes. It is chemotactic for neutrophils, monocytes and T cells through the receptor FPRL1 [3]. A mouse study found that a cathelicidin protects skin from invasive bacterial infection [4].

Vitamin D raises cathelicidin expression. Skin from people with atopic dermatitis was found to have lower LL-37 levels than psoriatic skin, linked to a higher susceptibility to skin infections [1]. Excess processed LL-37 is also suspected of contributing to rosacea and, bound to self nucleic acids, of sustaining inflammation in psoriasis. These roles are described in the Wikipedia article on cathelicidin.

Registered trials involving LL-37 are few and mostly observational or biomarker-based. A small phase 1/2 trial examined intratumoral LL-37 in melanoma (4 participants) [6]. A phase 2 trial of an LL-37 cream for diabetic foot ulcers (40 participants) is registered with unknown status [7]. Other registered studies measure endogenous LL-37 levels in periodontal and peri-implant disease and in smoking exposure [8][9]. None addresses acne, scarring or cosmetic skin outcomes.

Wikipedia notes that barriers to therapeutic use include rapid breakdown by proteases, limited bioavailability, production cost and restriction to injected or infused routes, and that modified analogues such as SAAP-148 are under study.

timeline.event: Term cathelicidin coined; a 39-residue peptide proposed.
Mature peptide shown to be LL-37, two residues shorter.
LL-37 shown to attract immune cells via FPRL1 [3].
Reduced LL-37 reported in atopic dermatitis skin [1].

lore.intro: Discussion on looksmax.org is sparse; one thread asks whether LL-37 helps acne [2].

claims.claim: LL-37 might help clear acne and heal skin
claims.believers: A forum poster asked whether others had used it to heal skin and clear acne, framing it against established acne treatments [2].
claims.experts: No published human studies have tested LL-37 for acne. Research concerns its natural role in skin immunity [1][5].

claims.believers: A reply in the same thread said it seems decent for anti-aging but with likely modest acute improvements, and another advised waiting for more research [2].
claims.experts: No clinical trials of LL-37 for skin aging were found.

card.summary: The body's own antimicrobial skin peptide, now chatted about for acne with no cosmetic trials behind it.
card.note: Not an approved drug; no acne or cosmetic trials found.

quick.overview:
LL-37 is a natural antimicrobial peptide made by skin and immune cells. Researchers study it mainly for its part in skin infection, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis and rosacea.

Some forum users ask about it for acne, but no human trial has tested that. The few registered LL-37 trials involve melanoma and diabetic foot ulcers.
quick.mechanism: It damages microbial membranes and attracts immune cells through the FPRL1 receptor. Vitamin D raises its production.
quick.risks: It is investigational. Wikipedia notes that excess LL-37 is suspected in rosacea and psoriasis inflammation. No safety data for cosmetic use were found.
